title: In a reverberant room, does PHAT win after all, and can the whitening exponent be chosen per window?
summary: Adds simulated reverberation (exponentially decaying Gaussian tails, RT60 0–1.0 s, direct-to-reverberant ratio +5 to −5 dB, Schroeder's statistical model) to capture-realaudio's 10 real clips and tests GCC delay estimators for camera audio sync. Across 20 cells (10 rooms, SNR −5 and +5 dB, 200 windows each), PHAT is the worst fixed weighting in 19 of 20 cells: at RT60 0.6 s, DRR 0 dB, SNR +5 dB it puts 0.26 of 2 s windows more than one 30 fps frame off, against 0.09 for partial whitening with γ = 0.5 and 0.20 for plain correlation. Choosing γ per window by peak-to-sidelobe ratio beats PHAT but not the best fixed γ; an oracle selector would roughly halve the failures again. Limits: statistical rooms rather than measured impulse responses, white noise, sound-effect clips, simulated delay.
lede: in a reverberant room, does PHAT win after all? No: across 10 simulated rooms PHAT is the worst fixed weighting; gamma 0.5 cuts failures from 0.26 to 0.09, and choosing gamma per window by peak-to-sidelobe ratio helps less than just fixing it.
